title: Given an array of non-negative values, pick a subset with the maximum total such that no two picked elements are adjacent. Explain the dynamic programming recurrence, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: House Robber (Maximum Sum of Non-Adjacent Elements)
keyPoints: At each element, choose the better of skipping it (keep previous best) or taking it (add to best from two back).
The recurrence is dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + values[i]), with dp[-1]=0 and dp[-2]=0.
Only the last two values are needed, so two rolling variables give O(1) space.
The circular variant (first and last also adjacent) runs the linear scan twice: once excluding first, once excluding last.
Time is O(n) for a single linear pass; brute-force subset enumeration would be O(2^n).
For monetary values, use long or BigDecimal to avoid overflow across many elements.

s1_definition.oneliner: At each element choose the better of skipping it or taking it plus the best from two back.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Binary decision** – at each index, either skip (keep dp[i-1]) or take (add value to dp[i-2]).
- **Recurrence** – `dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + values[i])`.
- **Rolling variables** – only dp[i-1] and dp[i-2] are needed, so `oneBack` and `twoBack` give O(1) space.
- **Circular variant** – first and last are also adjacent: run twice, excluding first then excluding last, take the max.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India runs a promotional cash-back on consecutive days, but a fraud rule forbids claiming cash-back on two back-to-back days. Rajesh picks the days that maximize his total cash-back without choosing two in a row.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  values: [2,  7,  9,  3,  1]

  Decision at each position:
  i=0: take 2                        best=2
  i=1: skip(2) vs take(0+7=7)       best=7
  i=2: skip(7) vs take(2+9=11)      best=11
  i=3: skip(11) vs take(7+3=10)     best=11
  i=4: skip(11) vs take(11+1=12)    best=12

  Selected: [2, 9, 1] → total 12
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
House Robber is the canonical maximum non-adjacent sum problem. At every position you face a binary decision: skip the current value and keep the previous best, or take the current value and add it to the best from two positions back. The answer at each position is the larger of the two options.

Since every decision looks only one and two positions behind, two rolling variables replace the entire DP table, giving linear time and constant space. This contrasts with the exponential cost of trying every subset.

The circular variant, where the first and last elements are also adjacent, is solved by running the linear scan twice: once excluding the first element and once excluding the last, taking the better result.

In a banking project at National Bank of India, a cash-back promotion forbade claiming on two consecutive days. The analytics team wanted the maximum total a customer could legitimately claim. The linear scan over daily values produced the answer, and the circular variant handled wrap-around promotions.

Remember one sentence: at each element, choose the better of skipping it or taking it plus the best from two back.
